newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan capital put on alert for "Heroes' Week".
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan capital put on alert for "Heroes' Week".

text.p: Security forces in the Sri Lankan capital Colombo were placed on full alert on Tuesday, the start of the separatist Tamil Tigers' "Heroes' Week", when the rebels traditionally stage attacks to honour fallen fighters, police said.

"Security measures have been tightened from today in view of the LTTE's Maha Veera Week," Colombo police chief D.M. Dissanayake said, referring to the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam's week-long commemoration of dead rebels.

"We have brought in additional forces from the outstations to strengthen Colombo's security. Many policemen and policewomen are patrolling the city in civvies (civilian clothes)," Dissanayake told Reuters.
For residents of this picturesque city of two million people on the shores of the Indian Ocean, the alert has meant delays from stepped up security checks and traffic jams due to road closures.
The measures added to the inconveniences that have became a fact of life for Colombo residents after two suicide bomb attacks blamed on the Tigers killed 140 people earlier this year.

The LTTE, waging a 13-year-old war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the island's north and east, has so far remained silent on the week, which culminates with the 42nd birthday of leader Velupillai Prabhakaran on November 26.
It has traditionally marked heroes' week, celebrating both the enigmatic Prabhakaran's birthday and the deaths of Tamil fighters, with attacks on military installations and remote border villages.

The rebels were not immediately available for comment on Tuesday. An LTTE radio station monitored in northern Sri Lankan announced only protests against government army restrictions on the movement of people and goods in the war zone.

But the military, which dealt the rebels a series of major blows when it drove them from key northern strongholds at Jaffna and Kilinochchi during the past year, said it was not taking heroes' week lightly.
"The anticipation is that the LTTE will carry out a big attack somewhere. And we have taken necessary steps to prevent it," said a military spokesman, who declined to be named.
"We do take this seriously," he said by telephone.

Two Colombo bombings this year blamed on the Tigers -- a January attack on the Central Bank that killed nearly 100 people and a July explosion at a suburban train station in which 40 died -- were retaliation for the army's capture of the LTTE's northern strongholds, analysts said.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the conflict, which began in 1983. The LTTE says a much larger number have died, most of them Tamils.
